Break Forth Before You Into Singing
BRAYK FORTH bee-FOR yoo IN-too SING-ing
n. phr. (the creation's welcome of the redeemed, Isaiah 55:12)
Hebrew yiphts'chū liphnēkem rinnāh — pātsach, to break out or burst forth, used of a sudden loud sound; rinnāh, a ringing cry, of joy or of supplication.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Isaiah closes the great invitation chapter with the manner of the return from exile: For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands. The figure is of creation itself greeting the redeemed as they pass. It is not mere decoration. Scripture holds that the ground was cursed for man's sake, that the creation was made subject to vanity not willingly, and that it groans and travails together until now, waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God. If the creation fell with man, it is fitting that it should rejoice at his deliverance, and Isaiah's next verse makes the link explicit by reversing the curse's own emblems: instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree. The singing mountains are therefore a statement about the scope of redemption. What Christ purchased is not the rescue of souls out of a doomed world but a new heaven and a new earth, and the hills that break forth into singing are the first sound of it. The verse ends by naming the purpose: it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Break forth, to burst out; to issue suddenly. Singing, uttering melodious sounds. Isaiah 55:12, creation greeting the redeemed on their way home.

expand to see more

Break forth, to burst out; to issue or come forth suddenly.

Sing, to utter sounds with musical inflections or modulations of voice.

Clap, to strike together with a quick motion, so as to make a noise.

Hebrew pātsach, to break out, burst forth into sound.

Hebrew rinnāh, a ringing cry of joy; also of entreaty. Isaiah 55:12.

Key Scripture

Isa 55:12 — "For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands."

Isa 55:13 — "Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off."

Rom 8:21 — "Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God."

Psa 98:8 — "Let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together"

Modern Corruption

The line is read as poetic ornament with no doctrine in it, or it is annexed to a nature-mysticism in which the creation is itself divine or self-redeeming.

expand to see more

Treated as ornament, the singing mountains are a pleasant flourish and the verse teaches nothing. Isaiah is making a claim. The creation is bound up with man's standing before God — cursed at his fall, groaning under the vanity it did not choose, and delivered at his redemption — and Paul states the same doctrine in plain prose in Romans 8. Where the claim is dropped, Christian hope quietly shrinks to the escape of the soul from the world, which is Plato's hope and not Isaiah's.

The opposite error annexes the verse to a reverence for nature in its own right, in which the earth is a living mother to be heard and heeded, and redemption is the restoration of a balance rather than the work of a Redeemer. Isaiah forecloses it in the next breath: the transformation is the LORD's doing, it is to the LORD for a name, and the trees do not sing of themselves but before the people whom He is leading out. The principle to recover is that the creation is a creature. It sings at the right time, for the right reason, and about Someone else.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pātsach, to burst forth into sound, with rinnāh, a ringing cry — the creation greeting a redeemed people and the curse's emblems reversed.

Hebrew pātsach, to break out or burst forth, of a sudden loud sound.

Hebrew rinnāh, a ringing cry, of joy or of supplication.

Hebrew māchā' kāph, to clap the hand — of the trees of the field.

The curse reversed: thorn to fir, brier to myrtle, Isaiah 55:13.

Paul states the doctrine in prose: the creation delivered, Romans 8:21.
